Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

items.content: Other Digital Payment Systems
items.exam_note: Section heading.

items.content: 1. NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer):

teacher_understanding.question: What does NEFT stand for?
teacher_understanding.answer: National Electronic Funds Transfer; it is the payment system introduced here for ordinary bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: What on this page identifies NEFT as a transfer system?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its expanded name refers to electronic funds transfer, and its bullets describe transfers in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a beginner understand electronic funds transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Money is moved through bank account records and electronic instructions rather than by physically carrying cash to the recipient.

prerequisites: sender and recipient of a payment
items.exam_note: Recognise the acronym and distinguish it from RTGS and IMPS.

terms.plain_meaning: नकद ले जाए बिना electronic तरीके से एक account से दूसरे में पैसे भेजना
terms.everyday_image: फोन से पैसे भेजने पर दूसरे के account में रकम दिखना

why_chain.step: A sender needs to pay someone without carrying cash.
NEFT offers electronic transfers and groups them in batches.

unpack.example_or_place: An ordinary transfer from one bank account to another.
unpack.consequence: The name identifies the system; its batch mechanism explains its speed.
unpack.visual_verb: move an electronic payment instruction between accounts
unpack.level_extra: Learn the expansion together with the distinguishing settlement mechanism.

items.content: • Available 24×7. Free of cost

teacher_understanding.question: What availability and cost does the prose assign to NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that NEFT is available 24×7 and free of cost.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the table support the availability statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes. The NEFT availability cell says '24×7, all days'; the table does not have a fee row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must availability not be confused with instant settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: A service may accept instructions throughout the day while settling them at scheduled intervals. Access time and processing time measure different things.

items.exam_note: Trap: 24×7 availability does not make NEFT an instant-settlement system.

terms.plain_meaning: दिन के 24 घंटे, हफ्ते के सातों दिन
terms.everyday_image: रविवार रात को भी transfer की सुविधा

why_chain.step: Payments may be needed outside branch opening hours.
The page says NEFT is available 24×7.

unpack.example_or_place: Submitting a transfer instruction on a Sunday evening.
unpack.consequence: Availability should be tested separately from speed and charges.
unpack.visual_verb: keep a weekly clock illuminated
unpack.level_extra: Keep the printed fee statement separate from any wider claim about all bank services.

items.content: • Transfers occur in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How does NEFT process transfers on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It groups transfers into batches rather than settling each separately as soon as it arrives.

teacher_understanding.question: When are these batches processed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies half-hourly batches, meaning batches at half-hour intervals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a batch-based transfer involve waiting?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction may arrive before the next batch is processed, so it waits for that processing round rather than being settled individually on arrival.

items.exam_note: Core NEFT–RTGS distinction; do not infer a guaranteed exact 30-minute credit time.

terms.plain_meaning: कई transfer को एक समूह में लेकर process करना
terms.everyday_image: लिफ्ट लोगों को इकट्ठा करके एक चक्कर में ले जाती है

why_chain.step: Many payment instructions need processing.
NEFT processes them in half-hourly groups.

unpack.example_or_place: Several account-transfer instructions entering a common processing round.
unpack.consequence: Batch processing explains the table's slower-speed description.
unpack.visual_verb: collect instructions and release successive batches
unpack.level_extra: Contrast continuous availability with periodic settlement.

items.content: • Suitable for ordinary bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: What use does the page associate with NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ordinary bank transfers, rather than the high-value urgent transfers emphasised for RTGS.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this use repeated?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table's Primary Use row describes NEFT as suitable for regular bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can batch processing suit an ordinary transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: When immediate receipt is not essential, a scheduled processing round can meet the payment need.

items.exam_note: Use-case matching is a common comparison format.

terms.plain_meaning: रोजमर्रा में account से पैसे भेजना, जहाँ तुरंत पहुँचना जरूरी न हो
terms.everyday_image: समय रहते किराए की रकम भेजना

why_chain.step: Some payments do not require immediate receipt.
The page associates regular transfers with NEFT.

unpack.example_or_place: A planned account-to-account payment.
unpack.consequence: Choose a system by urgency as well as amount.
unpack.visual_verb: match a routine payment to NEFT
unpack.level_extra: Suitability is not an exclusive legal restriction.

items.content: • Mainly for small amounts upto 5 lakh (Limit varies from bank to bank)

teacher_understanding.question: What amount guidance does the NEFT prose give?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes mainly small amounts upto 5 lakh and adds that the limit varies from bank to bank.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the table establish ₹5 lakh as a fixed NEFT maximum?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. The table says NEFT has 'No fixed limit', while the prose mentions 5 lakh with a bank-wise qualification. The page therefore does not support treating ₹5 lakh as an unqualified system-wide ceiling.

teacher_understanding.question: Why distinguish a bank's limit from a system-wide limit?
teacher_understanding.answer: A bank or access channel can impose an operational cap even when the payment system itself has a different limit framework.

items.exam_note: Preserve the internal qualification; avoid learning ₹5 lakh as an absolute NEFT ceiling.

terms.term: Limit varies from bank to bank
terms.plain_meaning: एक bank में जितनी रकम भेज सकते हैं, दूसरे में उतनी ही हो यह जरूरी नहीं
terms.everyday_image: दो banking apps में अलग transfer cap दिखना

why_chain.step: A sender must know whether the intended amount is permitted.
The prose gives bank-wise variation while the table gives no fixed NEFT maximum.

unpack.example_or_place: Checking the bank's transfer limit before sending a payment.
unpack.consequence: Read amount statements with their qualifications and source location.
unpack.visual_verb: place the prose limit beside the table's no-fixed-limit cell
unpack.level_extra: Internal source tension is explicit, not silently corrected.

items.content: Comparison Between NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, and UPI. Columns: criterion, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI. Rows: Full Form; Regulator; Settlement Type; Availability; Speed; Minimum Amount; Maximum Amount; Primary Use; Channels Supported.
items.exam_note: Children capture every comparison cell. Decorative phone and app pictures illustrate channels rather than a process diagram.

items.content: Full Form | NEFT: National Electronic Funds Transfer | RTGS: Real-Time Gross Settlement | IMPS: Immediate Payment Service | UPI: Unified Payments Interface

teacher_understanding.question: What do the four expanded names emphasise?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT names electronic funds transfer; RTGS names real-time gross settlement; IMPS names immediate payment service; UPI names a unified payments interface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which expansion uses 'Interface' rather than 'Transfer', 'Settlement' or 'Service'?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI expands to Unified Payments Interface, unlike the other three names.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the words help understanding rather than rote learning?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Real-time' directs attention to timing, 'gross' to individual settlement, and 'interface' to a way of accessing and initiating payments. The names highlight different aspects, not interchangeable systems.

items.exam_note: Acronym matching; preserve 'Payments' in UPI.

terms.plain_meaning: वह तरीका या जोड़ जिससे payment की सुविधा इस्तेमाल करते हैं
terms.everyday_image: फोन की app से payment शुरू करना

why_chain.step: Similar-looking acronyms can be confused.
Their full forms distinguish transfer, settlement, service and interface.

unpack.example_or_place: Recognising NEFT, RTGS and IMPS in a banking menu and UPI in a payment app.
unpack.consequence: Names become anchors for the later mechanism comparisons.
unpack.visual_verb: expand four acronyms into aligned names
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer identical mechanisms merely because all enable digital payments.

items.content: Regulator | NEFT: RBI | RTGS: RBI | IMPS: NPCI | UPI: NPCI

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table group the four systems institutionally?
teacher_understanding.answer: Under its 'Regulator' heading, it places NEFT and RTGS with RBI, and IMPS and UPI with NPCI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which pair shares the NPCI label rather than the RBI label?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS and UPI share NPCI; NEFT and RTGS share RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should the heading 'Regulator' be handled carefully?
teacher_understanding.answer: Regulation and operation are different roles. RBI regulates payment systems, while NPCI operates payment infrastructure including IMPS and UPI; the table's institutional pairing should not be taken to mean NPCI replaces RBI as statutory regulator.

items.exam_note: Institution matching is important; the printed 'Regulator' label simplifies distinct institutional roles.

terms.plain_meaning: नियम बनाने और पालन पर नजर रखने वाली संस्था
terms.everyday_image: खेल के नियम देखने वाला referee, खिलाड़ी नहीं

why_chain.step: Payment networks need institutions to run them and rules to govern them.
The table associates RBI with NEFT/RTGS and NPCI with IMPS/UPI.

unpack.example_or_place: An institution–payment-system matching question.
unpack.consequence: Retain the pairing without confusing an operator with the statutory regulator.
unpack.visual_verb: group four systems under two institution labels
unpack.level_extra: Outside clarification distinguishes oversight from network operation.

items.content: Settlement Type | NEFT: Batch-based (half-hourly) | RTGS: Real-time, gross settlement | IMPS: Real-time | UPI: Real-time

teacher_understanding.question: How does settlement type differ across the systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is batch-based at half-hour intervals. RTGS is real-time gross settlement; IMPS and UPI are labelled real-time.

teacher_understanding.question: What is distinctive about RTGS's wording?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS explicitly includes 'gross settlement', whereas IMPS and UPI cells state only 'Real-time'.

teacher_understanding.question: How does gross settlement differ from net settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Gross settlement settles each payment individually for its full amount. Net settlement offsets obligations and settles the resulting balance. Instant customer experience alone does not prove a particular interbank settlement model.

items.exam_note: Do not extend 'gross' from RTGS to every instant payment system.

terms.plain_meaning: हर payment को उसकी पूरी रकम के साथ अलग settle करना
terms.everyday_image: दो उधारों का फर्क निकालने के बजाय हर भुगतान अलग पूरा करना

why_chain.step: Payments need a way to discharge obligations between participating banks.
The table contrasts half-hourly NEFT batches with real-time descriptions.

unpack.example_or_place: Comparing a NEFT instruction with a high-value RTGS instruction.
unpack.consequence: Settlement design explains why equal availability does not imply equal processing.
unpack.visual_verb: contrast grouped instructions with individual settlement
unpack.level_extra: Separate customer-facing immediacy from the full interbank settlement architecture.

items.content: Availability | NEFT: 24×7, all days | RTGS: 24×7, all days | IMPS: 24×7, all days | UPI: 24×7, all days

teacher_understanding.question: What availability do the four systems share?
teacher_understanding.answer: Every column states 24×7 availability on all days.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this row distinguish NEFT from the other three?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Availability is the same in all four cells; their differences appear in settlement and speed rows.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is shared availability not shared speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Availability answers when a facility can be used; speed answers how quickly a payment is processed after initiation.

items.exam_note: A statement that singles out only one system as round-the-clock is not supported by this table.

terms.plain_meaning: किस समय सुविधा इस्तेमाल की जा सकती है
terms.everyday_image: दुकान खुली है या बंद, यह पूछना; सामान मिलने में कितना समय लगेगा, यह अलग सवाल है

why_chain.step: Users need payments beyond normal branch hours.
All four systems are shown as available around the clock.

unpack.example_or_place: A payment initiated on a public holiday.
unpack.consequence: Choose other criteria to distinguish the systems.
unpack.visual_verb: align four identical round-the-clock symbols
unpack.level_extra: The row is an availability statement, not a guarantee against technical downtime.

items.content: Speed | NEFT: Slower (batch processing) | RTGS: Instant for high-value | IMPS: Instant | UPI: Instant

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table rank payment speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: It calls NEFT slower because of batch processing, RTGS instant for high-value transfers, and IMPS and UPI instant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which system's speed is explicitly linked to batching?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT's slower speed is linked to batch processing, unlike the instant descriptions in the other columns.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can grouping transfers slow a particular instruction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The instruction may have to wait for its processing group, whereas individual immediate processing need not wait for a scheduled batch.

items.exam_note: Relate speed to mechanism rather than memorising isolated adjectives.

terms.plain_meaning: payment शुरू करने के बाद तुरंत होने वाला
terms.everyday_image: दुकानदार के फोन पर payment की सूचना तुरंत आना

why_chain.step: Some recipients need money immediately.
The table distinguishes slower NEFT batches from instant alternatives.

unpack.example_or_place: An urgent transfer contrasted with a planned routine payment.
unpack.consequence: Urgency guides the choice alongside amount limits.
unpack.visual_verb: show one instruction waiting and others moving immediately
unpack.level_extra: No exact seconds or guaranteed delivery time is supplied.

items.content: Minimum Amount | NEFT: No minimum | RTGS: 2 lakh | IMPS: No minimum | UPI: No minimum

teacher_understanding.question: How do minimum amounts compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is shown with a ₹2 lakh minimum. NEFT, IMPS and UPI are shown with no minimum.

teacher_understanding.question: Which entry is the exception to 'No minimum'?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is the exception, supporting the page's emphasis on high-value payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How consistent is the table's IMPS minimum with the prose?
teacher_understanding.answer: They differ: the table says 'No minimum', while the prose begins the IMPS range at ₹1. Both statements must be retained as printed.

items.exam_note: ₹2 lakh RTGS minimum is the key distinguishing number; flag the IMPS source discrepancy.

terms.plain_meaning: transfer के लिए बताई गई सबसे छोटी रकम
terms.everyday_image: किसी सुविधा के लिए कम-से-कम रकम की शर्त

why_chain.step: A proposed payment must meet any entry threshold.
The table specifies a 2 lakh threshold for RTGS.

unpack.example_or_place: Testing whether a hypothetical ₹50,000 payment meets the table's RTGS threshold.
unpack.consequence: RTGS is not the table's choice for a below-threshold amount.
unpack.visual_verb: place a ₹2 lakh threshold before the RTGS lane
unpack.level_extra: Keep 'no minimum' distinct from zero-value payments.

items.content: Maximum Amount | NEFT: No fixed limit | RTGS: No upper limit | IMPS: 5 lakh (varies by bank) | UPI: 1 lakh (default), 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant

teacher_understanding.question: What maximum amounts are printed in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT has no fixed limit; RTGS has no upper limit; IMPS has 5 lakh varying by bank; UPI has 1 lakh by default and 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which columns contain explicit numerical ceilings or differentiated limits?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS has a bank-qualified 5 lakh figure, and UPI distinguishes a default figure from a Person-to-Merchant figure. NEFT and RTGS have no numerical maximum in this row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the qualifications remain attached to these figures?
teacher_understanding.answer: A default amount, a category-specific amount and a bank-dependent cap are not equivalent universal limits. Removing the qualification changes the claim.

items.exam_note: Numbers are source claims, not independently verified current rules; the UPI 10 lakh claim should not be generalised beyond the printed wording.

terms.plain_meaning: किसी व्यक्ति का दुकानदार या कारोबार को payment करना
terms.everyday_image: किराने की दुकान पर QR से पैसे देना

terms.plain_meaning: आम तौर पर लागू बताई गई सीमा, खास category की अलग सीमा से पहले
terms.everyday_image: app की सामान्य setting और अलग खास setting

why_chain.step: A sender needs to know whether the full intended amount can be sent.
The table differentiates no-upper-limit entries from bank- and category-qualified figures.

unpack.example_or_place: Comparing an account transfer with a merchant payment.
unpack.consequence: Amount comparisons require both the number and its qualification.
unpack.visual_verb: attach qualification tags to each limit
unpack.level_extra: Contrast this NEFT cell explicitly with the prose's upto-5-lakh description.

items.content: Primary Use | NEFT: Regular bank transfers | RTGS: High-value, urgent transfers | IMPS: Urgent everyday transfers | UPI: Mobile-based, peer-to-peer & merchant payments

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table distinguish primary uses?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT serves regular bank transfers, RTGS high-value urgent transfers, IMPS urgent everyday transfers, and UPI mobile-based peer-to-peer and merchant payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How do RTGS and IMPS differ despite both being associated with urgency?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is specifically associated with high-value urgency; IMPS is associated with everyday urgent transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are UPI's peer-to-peer and merchant uses different?
teacher_understanding.answer: Peer-to-peer means paying another person, while a merchant payment pays a business for goods or services. The recipient's role differs even though the payment may use the same app.

items.exam_note: Match scenarios to primary uses; 'primary' does not mean exclusive.

terms.plain_meaning: एक व्यक्ति से दूसरे व्यक्ति को payment
terms.everyday_image: दोस्त को साझा खाने के अपने हिस्से के पैसे भेजना

why_chain.step: Payments differ in urgency, amount and recipient.
The table assigns a different primary-use description to each system.

unpack.example_or_place: A friend repayment, a shop payment and a high-value urgent bank transfer.
unpack.consequence: A realistic system choice combines purpose, speed and limits.
unpack.visual_verb: sort payment scenarios into four lanes
unpack.level_extra: Avoid treating examples of primary use as prohibitions on other uses.

items.content: Channels Supported | NEFT: Internet & mobile banking | RTGS: Internet & mobile banking | IMPS: Mobile banking, ATMs, & internet banking | UPI: Mobile apps (UPI apps like GPay, PhonePe)

teacher_understanding.question: What channels does the table list?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT and RTGS list internet and mobile banking. IMPS lists mobile banking, ATMs and internet banking. UPI lists mobile apps such as GPay and PhonePe.

teacher_understanding.question: Which column explicitly includes ATMs, and which names app examples?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS explicitly includes ATMs. UPI names GPay and PhonePe as app examples.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a channel differ from a payment system?
teacher_understanding.answer: A channel is the access route used to initiate a payment, such as a bank app or website. The payment system is the underlying arrangement through which the transfer is processed.

items.exam_note: Distinguish app brands, access channels and underlying systems.

terms.plain_meaning: किन रास्तों या सुविधाओं से payment शुरू कर सकते हैं
terms.everyday_image: एक ही काम के लिए website, phone app या ATM का दरवाजा चुनना

why_chain.step: A user needs a practical route to submit the payment instruction.
The table lists banking channels and UPI apps for this access.

unpack.example_or_place: Opening a bank app versus opening PhonePe.
unpack.consequence: Using a mobile phone does not by itself identify which underlying payment system is used.
unpack.visual_verb: connect access devices to the named systems
unpack.level_extra: Treat the listed channels as the table's entries, not necessarily exhaustive statements of all access possibilities.

items.content: 2. RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement):

teacher_understanding.question: What does RTGS mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stands for Real Time Gross Settlement, the system the page associates with instant high-value transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Which page statements unpack the expansion?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bullets specify real-time settlement and no batching, while the table describes real-time gross settlement.

teacher_understanding.question: How do 'real time' and 'gross' answer different questions?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Real time' describes when processing occurs; 'gross' describes settlement of individual payments for their full amounts rather than an offset net balance.

items.exam_note: Both timing and gross settlement matter in the expansion.

terms.plain_meaning: instruction आने पर उसी समय process होने वाला
terms.everyday_image: अगले समूह का इंतजार किए बिना एक व्यक्ति का काम लेना

why_chain.step: Some large payments require prompt completion.
RTGS is presented as real-time settlement without batching.

unpack.example_or_place: A high-value urgent bank transfer.
unpack.consequence: The expansion links directly to the NEFT–RTGS mechanism contrast.
unpack.visual_verb: split RTGS into timing and amount-settlement meanings
unpack.level_extra: Gross does not mean simply 'large'; it describes the settlement method.

items.content:
• Real-time settlement. Instant Process. Available 24×7.
• No batching.

teacher_understanding.question: How is RTGS settlement presented?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in real time as an instant process without batching, unlike NEFT's half-hourly groups.

teacher_understanding.question: When is RTGS available?
teacher_understanding.answer: The prose says 24×7, and the table adds 'all days'.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does 'no batching' help explain real-time processing?
teacher_understanding.answer: A payment need not wait for a scheduled collection of other instructions before being processed individually.

items.exam_note: Test timing, batching and availability as separate claims.

terms.plain_meaning: कई payment का समूह बनने का इंतजार नहीं
terms.everyday_image: पूरी बस भरने की जगह एक सवारी को तुरंत ले जाना

why_chain.step: An urgent payment should not depend on waiting for a group.
RTGS is described as instant and without batching.

unpack.example_or_place: A time-sensitive large transfer submitted through banking.
unpack.consequence: This mechanism supports RTGS's high-value urgent-use description.
unpack.visual_verb: settle instructions one by one as they arrive
unpack.level_extra: No processing-time guarantee in seconds is stated.

items.content: • Primarily used for high-value transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: What transaction category is RTGS primarily used for?
teacher_understanding.answer: High-value transactions; the table further describes them as urgent transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: What numerical entry reinforces this use?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table sets a 2 lakh minimum amount for RTGS.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is immediate settlement useful for a high-value payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: The recipient may be waiting to complete a major obligation, so prompt settlement reduces the period of uncertainty about receipt.

items.exam_note: Link high value to ₹2 lakh minimum, not to an imagined upper ceiling.

terms.plain_meaning: बड़ी रकम के payment
terms.everyday_image: किसी बड़ी खरीद की रकम account से भेजना

why_chain.step: A large payment may need prompt, definite completion.
The page associates RTGS with high-value urgent transfers.

unpack.consequence: RTGS differs from the table's urgent everyday IMPS use.

items.content: 1. NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer):

teacher_understanding.question: What does NEFT stand for?
teacher_understanding.answer: National Electronic Funds Transfer; it is the payment system introduced here for ordinary bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: What on this page identifies NEFT as a transfer system?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its expanded name refers to electronic funds transfer, and its bullets describe transfers in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a beginner understand electronic funds transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Money is moved through bank account records and electronic instructions rather than by physically carrying cash to the recipient.

prerequisites: sender and recipient of a payment
items.exam_note: Recognise the acronym and distinguish it from RTGS and IMPS.

items.content: • Available 24×7. Free of cost

teacher_understanding.question: What availability and cost does the prose assign to NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that NEFT is available 24×7 and free of cost.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the table support the availability statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes. The NEFT availability cell says '24×7, all days'; the table does not have a fee row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must availability not be confused with instant settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: A service may accept instructions throughout the day while settling them at scheduled intervals. Access time and processing time measure different things.

items.exam_note: Trap: 24×7 availability does not make NEFT an instant-settlement system.

terms.plain_meaning: दिन के 24 घंटे, हफ्ते के सातों दिन
terms.everyday_image: रविवार रात को भी transfer की सुविधा

The page says NEFT is available 24×7.

unpack.consequence: Availability should be tested separately from speed and charges.

items.content: • Transfers occur in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How does NEFT process transfers on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It groups transfers into batches rather than settling each separately as soon as it arrives.

teacher_understanding.question: When are these batches processed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies half-hourly batches, meaning batches at half-hour intervals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a batch-based transfer involve waiting?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction may arrive before the next batch is processed, so it waits for that processing round rather than being settled individually on arrival.

items.exam_note: Core NEFT–RTGS distinction; do not infer a guaranteed exact 30-minute credit time.

terms.plain_meaning: कई transfer को एक समूह में लेकर process करना
terms.everyday_image: लिफ्ट लोगों को इकट्ठा करके एक चक्कर में ले जाती है

why_chain.step: Many payment instructions need processing.
NEFT processes them in half-hourly groups.

unpack.consequence: Batch processing explains the table's slower-speed description.
unpack.visual_verb: collect instructions and release successive batches
unpack.level_extra: Contrast continuous availability with periodic settlement.

items.content: • Suitable for ordinary bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: What use does the page associate with NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ordinary bank transfers, rather than the high-value urgent transfers emphasised for RTGS.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this use repeated?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table's Primary Use row describes NEFT as suitable for regular bank transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can batch processing suit an ordinary transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: When immediate receipt is not essential, a scheduled processing round can meet the payment need.

items.exam_note: Use-case matching is a common comparison format.

items.content: Full Form | NEFT: National Electronic Funds Transfer | RTGS: Real-Time Gross Settlement | IMPS: Immediate Payment Service | UPI: Unified Payments Interface

teacher_understanding.question: What do the four expanded names emphasise?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT names electronic funds transfer; RTGS names real-time gross settlement; IMPS names immediate payment service; UPI names a unified payments interface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which expansion uses 'Interface' rather than 'Transfer', 'Settlement' or 'Service'?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI expands to Unified Payments Interface, unlike the other three names.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the words help understanding rather than rote learning?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Real-time' directs attention to timing, 'gross' to individual settlement, and 'interface' to a way of accessing and initiating payments. The names highlight different aspects, not interchangeable systems.

items.exam_note: Acronym matching; preserve 'Payments' in UPI.

Their full forms distinguish transfer, settlement, service and interface.

unpack.example_or_place: Recognising NEFT, RTGS and IMPS in a banking menu and UPI in a payment app.
unpack.consequence: Names become anchors for the later mechanism comparisons.
unpack.visual_verb: expand four acronyms into aligned names
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer identical mechanisms merely because all enable digital payments.

items.content: Regulator | NEFT: RBI | RTGS: RBI | IMPS: NPCI | UPI: NPCI

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table group the four systems institutionally?
teacher_understanding.answer: Under its 'Regulator' heading, it places NEFT and RTGS with RBI, and IMPS and UPI with NPCI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which pair shares the NPCI label rather than the RBI label?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS and UPI share NPCI; NEFT and RTGS share RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: What does NPCI stand for, and what does it do?
teacher_understanding.answer: NPCI stands for National Payments Corporation of India. It operates retail-payment infrastructure, including IMPS and UPI, that enables participating banks and payment applications to connect for payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How does NPCI's role connect to a familiar UPI payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: When a customer pays a shop through a UPI app, the app is the visible access point. NPCI operates the underlying UPI network connecting participants; it is not simply the app the customer sees.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the table's 'Regulator' heading misleading for NPCI?
teacher_understanding.answer: Operating payment infrastructure and regulating payment systems are different jobs. RBI is the payment-system regulator, while NPCI operates infrastructure such as IMPS and UPI under regulatory oversight. NPCI does not replace RBI as statutory regulator.

prerequisites: payment apps versus underlying payment networks
items.exam_note: Learn NPCI's expansion and the institutional pairings, but do not reproduce the table's operator–regulator confusion.

items.content: Settlement Type | NEFT: Batch-based (half-hourly) | RTGS: Real-time, gross settlement | IMPS: Real-time | UPI: Real-time

teacher_understanding.question: How does settlement type differ across the systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is batch-based at half-hour intervals. RTGS is real-time gross settlement; IMPS and UPI are labelled real-time.

teacher_understanding.question: What is distinctive about RTGS's wording?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS explicitly includes 'gross settlement', whereas IMPS and UPI cells state only 'Real-time'.

teacher_understanding.question: How does gross settlement differ from net settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Gross settlement settles each payment individually for its full amount. Net settlement offsets obligations and settles the resulting balance. Instant customer experience alone does not prove a particular interbank settlement model.

items.exam_note: Do not extend 'gross' from RTGS to every instant payment system.

why_chain.step: Payments need a way to discharge obligations between participating banks.

unpack.level_extra: Separate customer-facing immediacy from the full interbank settlement architecture.

items.content: Availability | NEFT: 24×7, all days | RTGS: 24×7, all days | IMPS: 24×7, all days | UPI: 24×7, all days

teacher_understanding.question: What availability do the four systems share?

teacher_understanding.question: Does this row distinguish NEFT from the other three?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Availability is the same in all four cells; their differences appear in settlement and speed rows.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is shared availability not shared speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Availability answers when a facility can be used; speed answers how quickly a payment is processed after initiation.

items.exam_note: A statement that singles out only one system as round-the-clock is not supported by this table.

items.content: Speed | NEFT: Slower (batch processing) | RTGS: Instant for high-value | IMPS: Instant | UPI: Instant

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table rank payment speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: It calls NEFT slower because of batch processing, RTGS instant for high-value transfers, and IMPS and UPI instant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which system's speed is explicitly linked to batching?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT's slower speed is linked to batch processing, unlike the instant descriptions in the other columns.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can grouping transfers slow a particular instruction?
teacher_understanding.answer: The instruction may have to wait for its processing group, whereas individual immediate processing need not wait for a scheduled batch.

items.exam_note: Relate speed to mechanism rather than memorising isolated adjectives.

items.content: Minimum Amount | NEFT: No minimum | RTGS: 2 lakh | IMPS: No minimum | UPI: No minimum

teacher_understanding.question: How do minimum amounts compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is shown with a ₹2 lakh minimum. NEFT, IMPS and UPI are shown with no minimum.

teacher_understanding.question: Which entry is the exception to 'No minimum'?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is the exception, supporting the page's emphasis on high-value payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How consistent is the table's IMPS minimum with the prose?
teacher_understanding.answer: They differ: the table says 'No minimum', while the prose begins the IMPS range at ₹1. Both statements must be retained as printed.

items.exam_note: ₹2 lakh RTGS minimum is the key distinguishing number; flag the IMPS source discrepancy.

terms.plain_meaning: transfer के लिए बताई गई सबसे छोटी रकम

items.content: Maximum Amount | NEFT: No fixed limit | RTGS: No upper limit | IMPS: 5 lakh (varies by bank) | UPI: 1 lakh (default), 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant

teacher_understanding.question: What maximum amounts are printed in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT has no fixed limit; RTGS has no upper limit; IMPS has 5 lakh varying by bank; UPI has 1 lakh by default and 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which columns contain explicit numerical ceilings or differentiated limits?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS has a bank-qualified 5 lakh figure, and UPI distinguishes a default figure from a Person-to-Merchant figure. NEFT and RTGS have no numerical maximum in this row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must qualifications remain attached to transaction limits?
teacher_understanding.answer: A default amount, a category-specific amount and a bank-dependent cap are not equivalent universal limits. Removing the qualification changes the claim.

teacher_understanding.question: Is the printed ₹10 lakh figure a universal ceiling available for every UPI merchant payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. The table's blanket Person-to-Merchant wording is misleading. Enhanced UPI limits apply to specified eligible categories and conditions, not automatically to every merchant payment. ₹10 lakh must not be taught as a universal P2M ceiling.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a learner assess whether an enhanced UPI limit applies to a particular payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: Check whether the payment falls within an eligible category and meets the applicable conditions, including relevant bank or app restrictions. A merchant recipient alone does not establish eligibility for an enhanced limit.

items.exam_note: Preserve the printed figures as source content, but reject the claim that every UPI P2M payment has a ₹10 lakh ceiling. Enhanced limits require eligible categories and conditions.

terms.everyday_image: सामान्य entry ticket और खास शर्तों वाला अलग pass

items.content: Primary Use | NEFT: Regular bank transfers | RTGS: High-value, urgent transfers | IMPS: Urgent everyday transfers | UPI: Mobile-based, peer-to-peer & merchant payments

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table distinguish primary uses?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT serves regular bank transfers, RTGS high-value urgent transfers, IMPS urgent everyday transfers, and UPI mobile-based peer-to-peer and merchant payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How do RTGS and IMPS differ despite both being associated with urgency?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is specifically associated with high-value urgency; IMPS is associated with everyday urgent transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are UPI's peer-to-peer and merchant uses different?
teacher_understanding.answer: Peer-to-peer means paying another person, while a merchant payment pays a business for goods or services. The recipient's role differs even though the payment may use the same app.

items.exam_note: Match scenarios to primary uses; 'primary' does not mean exclusive.

terms.everyday_image: दोस्त को साझा खाने के अपने हिस्से के पैसे भेजना

why_chain.step: Payments differ in urgency, amount and recipient.
The table assigns a different primary-use description to each system.

unpack.example_or_place: A friend repayment, a shop payment and a high-value urgent bank transfer.
unpack.consequence: A realistic system choice combines purpose, speed and limits.
unpack.visual_verb: sort payment scenarios into four lanes
unpack.level_extra: Avoid treating examples of primary use as prohibitions on other uses.

items.content: Channels Supported | NEFT: Internet & mobile banking | RTGS: Internet & mobile banking | IMPS: Mobile banking, ATMs, & internet banking | UPI: Mobile apps (UPI apps like GPay, PhonePe)

teacher_understanding.question: What channels does the table list?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT and RTGS list internet and mobile banking. IMPS lists mobile banking, ATMs and internet banking. UPI lists mobile apps such as GPay and PhonePe.

teacher_understanding.question: Which column explicitly includes ATMs, and which names app examples?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS explicitly includes ATMs. UPI names GPay and PhonePe as app examples.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a channel differ from a payment system?
teacher_understanding.answer: A channel is the access route used to initiate a payment, such as a bank app or website. The payment system is the underlying arrangement through which the transfer is processed.

items.exam_note: Distinguish app brands, access channels and underlying systems.

terms.plain_meaning: किन रास्तों या सुविधाओं से payment शुरू कर सकते हैं

why_chain.step: A user needs a practical route to submit the payment instruction.
The table lists banking channels and UPI apps for this access.

unpack.example_or_place: Opening a bank app versus opening PhonePe.
unpack.consequence: Using a mobile phone does not by itself identify which underlying payment system is used.
unpack.visual_verb: connect access devices to the named systems
unpack.level_extra: Treat the listed channels as the table's entries, not necessarily exhaustive statements of all access possibilities.

items.content: 2. RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement):

teacher_understanding.question: What does RTGS mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: It stands for Real Time Gross Settlement, the system the page associates with instant high-value transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Which page statements unpack the expansion?
teacher_understanding.answer: The bullets specify real-time settlement and no batching, while the table describes real-time gross settlement.

teacher_understanding.question: How do 'real time' and 'gross' answer different questions?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Real time' describes when processing occurs; 'gross' describes settlement of individual payments for their full amounts rather than an offset net balance.

items.exam_note: Both timing and gross settlement matter in the expansion.

RTGS is presented as real-time settlement without batching.

unpack.example_or_place: A high-value urgent bank transfer.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is immediate settlement useful for a high-value payment?

items.content: 3. IMPS (Immediate Payment Service):

teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS is the payment service; mobile banking is one access channel through which a customer can use it.

teacher_understanding.question: How does NEFT process transfers on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It groups transfers into batches rather than settling each separately as soon as it arrives.

teacher_understanding.question: When are these batches processed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies half-hourly batches, meaning batches at half-hour intervals.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a batch-based transfer involve waiting?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction may arrive before the next batch is processed, so it waits for that processing round rather than being settled individually on arrival.

items.content: Full Form | NEFT: National Electronic Funds Transfer | RTGS: Real-Time Gross Settlement | IMPS: Immediate Payment Service | UPI: Unified Payments Interface

teacher_understanding.question: What do the four expanded names emphasise?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT names electronic funds transfer; RTGS names real-time gross settlement; IMPS names immediate payment service; UPI names a unified payments interface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which expansion uses 'Interface' rather than 'Transfer', 'Settlement' or 'Service'?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI expands to Unified Payments Interface, unlike the other three names.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the words help understanding rather than rote learning?
teacher_understanding.answer: 'Real-time' directs attention to timing, 'gross' to individual settlement, and 'interface' to a way of accessing and initiating payments. The names highlight different aspects, not interchangeable systems.

unpack.consequence: Names become anchors for the later mechanism comparisons.
unpack.visual_verb: expand four acronyms into aligned names
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer identical mechanisms merely because all enable digital payments.

items.content: Regulator | NEFT: RBI | RTGS: RBI | IMPS: NPCI | UPI: NPCI

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table group the four systems institutionally?
teacher_understanding.answer: Under its 'Regulator' heading, it places NEFT and RTGS with RBI, and IMPS and UPI with NPCI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which pair shares the NPCI label rather than the RBI label?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS and UPI share NPCI; NEFT and RTGS share RBI.

teacher_understanding.question: What does NPCI stand for, and what does it do?
teacher_understanding.answer: NPCI stands for National Payments Corporation of India. It operates retail-payment infrastructure, including IMPS and UPI, that enables participating banks and payment applications to connect for payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How does NPCI's role connect to a familiar UPI payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: When a customer pays a shop through a UPI app, the app is the visible access point. NPCI operates the underlying UPI network connecting participants; it is not simply the app the customer sees.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the table's 'Regulator' heading misleading for NPCI?
teacher_understanding.answer: Operating payment infrastructure and regulating payment systems are different jobs. RBI is the payment-system regulator, while NPCI operates infrastructure such as IMPS and UPI under regulatory oversight. NPCI does not replace RBI as statutory regulator.
